A Treatise on Different Dice-rolling Mechanics in RPGs

An interesting read on what a "perfect" dice mechanic would have and then looks at how D&D, World of Darkness, and Fudge stack up.

The short version is the 3 ingredients to a "perfect" i.e. bell curve dice mechanic:

  1. Speed and ease-of-use. Any resolution should be quickly and easely achieved.
  2. Precision. Any factor should be highly measurable, allowing for small variances in factors.
  3. Correctness. The mechanic should come as close as possible to our intuitive understanding of the Degree of Success distribution — specifically the DoS distributions should look at least something like that of figure 1.

I think these are good criteria to use when designing your own mechanics, even though #3 is pretty subjective, but I disagree with the bell curve as "perfect". Or at least the standard distribution. It's only perfect for a true random distribution, but your PC's are not random. Even trying something your not skilled at is not truly random. You would use knowledge/skills in other areas and try to apply them to the current issue. You may have never swung a sword before, but you would know where the handle is and that the pointy end goes in the other guy. I think a "perfect" system, at least a better system wouldn't have a perfect bell curve, i.e. standard distribution, but more of a "spiked" distribution. If you're an avg PC, then 90% of your rolls should be a 10 (on a D20). While there is still some randomness, you should be pretty confident in what a roll will be before it happens. Your average car driver will not catastrophically fail to keep the car on the road nor pull off some supremely awesome maneuver. They will just get from point A to B >90% of the time. As you get better at any skill that spike should get tighter.

While this is mathematicaly interesting, not including the rest of the rules takes a lot of the supporting mechanics out of consideration.

Fudge, for instance, allows for re-rolling, or increasing ones roll by spending Fudge points. This changes the game in ways that aren't the same as D&D.

This article doesn't consider the differing types of games. It only considers that the best games are like simulators, trying to mimic the real world in a mechanical way, rather than in the way it feels, or a dramatic way.

Fudge is a good example, since it let's the players "cheat" the physics of the dice rolls, which adds drama, making actions more likely to succeed in a heroic way.

Another game, Fate, takes Fudge another step and has characters fail in heroic ways, too. This makes for a less realistic game, but pushes for a more dramatic game.

For me, and this is an oppinion, the dice mechanics considered in the article only apply to simulation of physics, which isn't really pushing for something interesting or fun. I do understand that others get enjoyment from simulation based gaming, but for me, the escapist part of gaming is very important. I want my characters to be intentionally heroic.

This is a good lesson on making sure the dice mechanics fit the tone of the game. If you were trying to make a game in a Matrix style universe a die system like Fudge/Fate would better fit the world and play style. If you were making a Black Hawk Down game, a more mechanical realistic dice system would be better, as the tone is not about being an over the top action hero but about realism and strategy, as one hit could take you out.

Very interesting. I'm a fan of old technology and I really like vacuum tubes so this would be pretty sweet, especially if it means better performance and not just nostalgia factor. That said, hopefully this won't increase production costs too much.

Also:

Still, she cautions, the nano vacuum tube is more of a "proof of concept" than a working device, since its operational requirements do not yet match modern transistors. As one example, about 10 volts is needed to switch the device on, whereas modern transistors operate at about 1 volt; in this respect, the nano vacuum tube isn't compatible with modern circuits.

So it looks like it's got a while to go before we start seeing it implemented in anything. I'll be keeping an eye on this.

While this is certainly not nano-scale tube technology, Korg and Noritake recently announced a new direction for adding tubes to modern devices. It's based on Vacuum Fluorescent Display technology and can be mass produced in modern VFD manufacturing lines. The size, power requirements and long life will certainly see it used in many audio applications and eventually replacing classic tubes like the 12AX7. Korg has used tubes in a variety of synthesizers over recent years to give them richness and gritty sounds so it seems like a logical step for them. As an electronic hobbyist, I look forward to playing around with these little tubes when they become mass market. Plus to me they just look cool (because I love VFDs).

If you went back in time to when transistors were new, and you told them that in 70 years, transistors would be obsolete, replaced by 2 technologies, one of which is vacuum tubes, and the other being essentially magic, they probably wouldn't believe you.
